title: Computer Rental
description: Computer rental costs are amounts paid for the right to use computers, including cloud IaaS and PaaS, in qualified research under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii).
summary: Computer rental costs are amounts U.S. taxpayers pay another person for the right to use computers, including cloud IaaS and PaaS, in qualified research under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii). They count as 100% in-house QREs for R&D tax credits, but only if the computers are third-party owned, off-premises, not primarily used by the taxpayer, with costs allocated to research.

body.text: Computer rental costs are amounts U.S. taxpayers pay another person for the right to use computers, including cloud IaaS and PaaS, in qualified research under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii). They count as 100% in-house QREs for R&D tax credits, but only if the computers are third-party owned, off-premises, not primarily used by the taxpayer, with costs allocated to research.

Payments for the rental or lease of computers used directly in qualified research represent a foundational—yet frequently misapplied—component of the U.S. Research and Development (R&D) Tax Credit under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 41. Authorized by IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii), taxpayers may treat "any amount paid or incurred to another person for the right to use computers in the conduct of qualified research" as an in-house Qualified Research Expense (QRE). Originally enacted to accommodate time-sharing on off-site mainframe computers, this statutory provision now serves as the primary legal mechanism for claiming modern cloud computing expenditures—specifically Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) and Platform as a Service (PaaS) environments hosted by third-party Cloud Service Providers (CSPs) such as Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud. Because qualified computer rental expenses are classified as in-house QREs, they are eligible for a 100% inclusion rate in the QRE base, offering a 35 percentage point advantage over general Contract Research Expenses, which are capped at a 65% inclusion rate under IRC § 41(b)(3)(A) and Treasury Regulation (Treas. Reg.) § 1.41-2(e)(1).

To qualify as a computer rental QRE, an expenditure must satisfy both the activity-level four-part test for Qualified Research Activities (QRAs) under IRC § 41(d)(1) and the strict three-part regulatory test under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b)(4), which mandates that the computer be (1) owned and operated by someone other than the taxpayer, (2) located off the taxpayer's premises, and (3) not primarily used by the taxpayer. Furthermore, unlike employee wages—which benefit from an 80% "substantially all" inclusion rule under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d)(2)—computer rental expenses enjoy no blanket inclusion safe harbor. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b)(1), taxpayers must strictly segregate and allocate cloud computing costs between eligible research activities (such as pre-release software development, code compilation, and computational simulation) and ineligible commercial production hosting or general and administrative (G&A) functions.

items: Regulatory Promulgation Date: Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b)(4) was promulgated on May 17, 1989, under Treasury Decision (T.D.) 8251 (54 FR 21204; subsequently amended by T.D. 8930, 65 FR 287, Jan. 3, 2001), not in 1985; the 1985 reference reflects the post-December 31, 1985 statutory effective date established by the Tax Reform Act of 1986 (Public Law 99-514).

Statutory Reduction Clause and "Substantially All" Contradiction: The flush language of IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii) contains a mandatory reduction clause disqualifying computer rental payments to the extent the taxpayer (or any person with whom the taxpayer must aggregate expenditures under IRC § 41(f)(1)) receives or accrues any amount from any other person for the right to use substantially identical personal property.

Contract Research Inclusion Tiers: While the general inclusion rate for contract research expenses is 65% under IRC § 41(b)(3)(A) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)(1), the statute provides a 75% inclusion rate for amounts paid to qualified research consortia under IRC § 41(b)(3)(C) and a 100% inclusion rate for eligible energy research payments made to eligible small businesses, universities, or federal laboratories under IRC § 41(b)(3)(D).

Form 6765 Section G Effective Dates, Exemptions, and Narrative Rules: Itemized business component reporting on Form 6765, Section G (where computer rental costs are reported on Line/Column 55 and summed on Section F, Line 44) is optional for all filers for tax years beginning before 2026 and becomes mandatory only for tax years beginning after 2025. Even for tax years beginning after 2025, exemptions apply to Qualified Small Businesses (QSBs) electing the reduced payroll tax credit under IRC § 41(h) and to taxpayers claiming the credit on an original return with total controlled-group QREs equal to or less than $1.5 million and prior three-year average annual gross receipts equal to or less than $50 million. Moreover, narrative descriptions of the information sought to be discovered in Section G, Column 49(f) are required only on amended returns claiming a new or increased research credit, not on timely filed original returns.

Scope of the 2025 Final Cloud Regulations (T.D. 10022): Final regulations published on January 14, 2025 (T.D. 10022, 90 FR 2977; Treas. Reg. §§ 1.861-18 and 1.861-19) classify all cloud transactions (IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS) solely as the provision of services rather than leases of property, but Section VI of the preamble explicitly restricts this classification to enumerated international tax provisions of the Code. Through Notice 2025-6 (2025-8 I.R.B. 799), Treasury and the IRS are evaluating whether to extend Treas. Reg. §§ 1.861-18 and 1.861-19 across all provisions of the Internal Revenue Code—a step that, without a concurrent IRC § 41 carve-out or regulatory update, could conflict with treating cloud computing as a 100% in-house computer rental expense.

body.text: Statutory and Regulatory Framework for Computer Rental QREs
In-House Research Expense Classification Under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(A)(iii)

Under IRC § 41(b)(1), a taxpayer's total Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) equal the sum of "in-house research expenses" and "contract research expenses" paid or incurred by the taxpayer during the taxable year in carrying on any trade or business of the taxpayer. IRC § 41(b)(2)(A) defines in-house research expenses as comprising three exhaustive statutory categories: (i) any "wages" (as defined in IRC § 3401(a), including self-employed earned income under IRC § 401(c)(2) per IRC § 41(b)(2)(D)(ii), but excluding amounts taken into account in determining the work opportunity credit under IRC § 51(a) per IRC § 41(b)(2)(D)(iii)) paid or incurred to an employee for "qualified services" performed by such employee (IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(i), (B), (D)); (ii) any amount paid or incurred for "supplies" used in the conduct of qualified research (IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii)); and (iii) "under regulations prescribed by the Secretary, any amount paid or incurred to another person for the right to use computers in the conduct of qualified research" (IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii)). Under IRC § 41(b)(4), in the case of in-house research expenses, a startup venture is treated as meeting the trade or business requirement of IRC § 41(b)(1) if, at the time such in-house research expenses are paid or incurred, the principal purpose of the taxpayer in making such expenditures is to use the results of the research in the active conduct of a future trade or business of the taxpayer or an aggregated group member under IRC § 41(f)(1). If an expenditure does not fall within one of the three in-house categories of IRC § 41(b)(2) or contract research under IRC § 41(b)(3), the IRS Audit Techniques Guide (ATG) for IRC § 41 Qualified Research Expenses emphasizes that a taxpayer may not claim the expenditure as a QRE.

The computer rental provision fulfills a vital structural role within the statutory architecture of IRC § 41. Under IRC § 41(b)(2)(C), the term "supplies" means any tangible property other than (i) land or improvements to land, and (ii) property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation. Similarly, under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b)(2)(i)–(ii), general building utilities (water, electricity, and natural gas) are treated as ineligible G&A expenses unless the taxpayer establishes extraordinary utility expenditures required by the special character of the qualified research (such as high-energy laser or nuclear research). Because purchased computer hardware, workstations, and on-premises physical servers are tangible property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation under IRC §§ 167 and 168, neither their capital acquisition cost nor their annual Modified Accelerated Cost Recovery System (MACRS) depreciation allowance can be claimed as a supply QRE under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii). By enacting IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii), Congress established a dedicated statutory mechanism permitting taxpayers that rent or lease computing capacity from third parties—rather than purchasing depreciable computer hardware outright—to include those usage payments as in-house QREs.

However, an audit of the statutory text in IRC § 41(b)(2)(A) reveals a mandatory statutory offset in the flush language of IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii) that must be applied whenever computer rental QREs are claimed. Specifically, the statute provides that Clause (iii) "shall not apply to any amount to the extent that the taxpayer (or any person with whom the taxpayer must aggregate expenditures under subsection (f)(1)) receives or accrues any amount from any other person for the right to use substantially identical personal property". In accordance with this statutory mandate, the official IRS Instructions for Form 6765 explicitly direct taxpayers to reduce their claimed rental or lease cost of computers by any amount that the taxpayer—or any member of a controlled group of corporations or businesses under common control under IRC § 41(f)(1)—received or accrued for granting another party the right to use substantially identical computing property.

The financial significance of qualifying cloud computing expenditures under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii) rather than IRC § 41(b)(3) stems directly from the statutory inclusion rates. In-house research expenses under IRC § 41(b)(2)—including qualified computer rentals—are included in the QRE calculation at 100% of the eligible expenditure. By contrast, under IRC § 41(b)(3)(A) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)(1), "contract research expenses" paid or incurred to any person other than an employee of the taxpayer for the performance on the taxpayer's behalf of qualified research (or services that, if performed by employees, would constitute qualified services under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B)) are generally limited to 65% of the qualified amount (and under IRC § 41(b)(3)(B), prepaid contract research attributable to research conducted after the close of the taxable year is deferred until the period in which the research is actually conducted). While IRC § 41(b)(3) contains two specialized statutory tiers—a 75% inclusion rate under IRC § 41(b)(3)(C) for amounts paid to a tax-exempt IRC § 501(c)(3) or § 501(c)(6) "qualified research consortium" conducting scientific research on behalf of the taxpayer and one or more unrelated taxpayers, and a 100% inclusion rate under IRC § 41(b)(3)(D) for amounts paid to eligible small businesses (500 or fewer employees and less than 50% owned by the taxpayer), institutions of higher education (as defined in IRC § 3304(f)), or federal laboratories (as defined in 15 U.S.C. § 3703(6)) for "qualified energy research"—payments to commercial cloud vendors do not qualify for those exceptions. Consequently, when a taxpayer properly substantiates commercial cloud computing costs as in-house computer rentals under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii) rather than misclassifying them as general contract research under IRC § 41(b)(3)(A) (a frequent compliance error highlighted by practitioner analyses such as McGuire Sponsel), the taxpayer preserves 35% of the qualifying expenditure in its QRE base.
Historical Evolution and the Three-Part Test of Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(b)(4)

Understanding how IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii) applies to contemporary cloud computing architectures requires tracing its legislative and regulatory evolution—and correcting a chronological misconception found in secondary commentary. When Congress first enacted the R&D tax credit in the Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981 (ERTA, P.L. 97-34, originally codified at IRC § 44F(b)(2)(A)(iii)), in-house QREs broadly encompassed amounts paid to unrelated third parties for the right to use any personal property in the conduct of qualified research. In the Tax Reform Act of 1986 (P.L. 99-514), effective for taxable years beginning after December 31, 1985, Congress repealed general personal property rental eligibility and narrowed the statutory provision strictly to amounts paid or incurred for the right to use computers in the conduct of qualified research under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii). As explained in the Joint Committee on Taxation's General Explanation of the Tax Reform Act of 1986 (JCS-10-87, May 15, 1987, p. 130), research computers in that era consisted of large, capital-intensive mainframe supercomputers; Congress preserved eligibility for computer usage payments to assist smaller businesses that could not afford to purchase or lease entire mainframe systems outright and instead rented processing time via remote terminals.

In fact, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b)(4) was not issued in 1985. Exercising the explicit rulemaking delegation in IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii), the Treasury Department promulgated Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b)(4) on May 17, 1989, in T.D. 8251 (54 FR 21204; subsequently amended by T.D. 8930, 65 FR 287 / 66 FR 289, Jan. 3, 2001), implementing the Tax Reform Act of 1986 statutory rules that took effect for taxable years beginning after December 31, 1985.

The verbatim text of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b)(4), titled Use of personal property in taxable years beginning after December 31, 1985 (right to use time-sharing computers), establishes the controlling regulatory standard:

"For taxable years beginning after December 31, 1985, amounts paid or incurred for the use of personal property are not qualified research expenses, except for any amount paid or incurred to another person for the right to use (time-sharing) computers in the conduct of qualified research. The computer must be owned and operated by someone other than the taxpayer, located off the taxpayer's premises, and the taxpayer must not be the primary user of the computer."

Notably, the regulation explicitly incorporates the parenthetical modifier "(time-sharing) computers", reflecting the 1960s–1980s computing architecture in which multiple unrelated users connected stationary terminals to a central processing unit (CPU). Neither IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii) nor Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b)(4) has been revised since 1989, and the IRS Audit Techniques Guide merely restates the statutory rule. Consequently, modern cloud computing claims must satisfy each prong of this three-part regulatory test. First, the physical server infrastructure and underlying hardware management layer must be legally owned and operated by someone other than the taxpayer, distinguishing a genuine computer usage arrangement from taxpayer-owned depreciable hardware or a capital/operating equipment lease where the taxpayer operates the physical server hardware itself. Second, the actual computer processing and physical server racks must be physically situated off the taxpayer's premises at a remote third-party facility—a condition readily satisfied by public cloud data centers, provided those data centers are located within the United States, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or U.S. territories per IRC § 41(d)(4)(F) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(7). Third, the taxpayer must not be the primary user of the computer, ensuring that the claimed expenditure reflects the rental of a shared or pooled computing resource serving multiple consumers rather than proprietary monopolization of an entire dedicated computer system.

From an audit defense perspective, the third criterion—the non-primary user requirement—is the most technically nuanced element during an IRS examination of cloud computing expenditures. As the IRS explains in its official Cloud Computing Environment guidance, a defining technical characteristic of cloud architecture is "resource pooling" via a multi-tenant model, wherein a provider's physical and virtual computing resources (storage, processing, memory, and network bandwidth) are pooled to serve multiple consumers and dynamically assigned and reassigned according to consumer demand. When a taxpayer provisions virtual machines (such as AWS EC2 instances) in a public cloud, the workload is routed dynamically across shared infrastructure, and the underlying physical server hardware, hypervisors, network fabric, and data center facilities remain owned, operated, and shared across multiple unrelated tenants of the CSP.

However, as tax practitioners point out in The Tax Adviser and industry analyses, the Internal Revenue Code does not formally define "primary user" for purposes of IRC § 41. In the context of depreciation, "primary use" of property is generally established by any reasonable method consistently applied (Treas. Reg. § 1.168(i)-4(d)(2)(i)), often interpreted as a greater-than-50% usage threshold. While classic 1980s mainframe time-sharing made it straightforward to measure whether one user consumed more than 50% of a central processor's time, modern private cloud or dedicated single-tenant bare-metal server arrangements require closer scrutiny. According to practitioner commentary, if a company pays for dedicated physical servers in a private cloud where the servers are devoted exclusively to that taxpayer's use 24/7 or where the taxpayer inspects or maintains the hardware, an IRS examiner may challenge whether the taxpayer is the "primary user" or operator. Conversely, if the taxpayer rents flexible capacity across a large data center where server allocation is dynamic and governed by the CSP—and where the taxpayer's use of any specific physical server does not exceed 50% of its capacity or useful life—the analogy to classic time-sharing holds. Taxpayers should therefore retain CSP architectural documentation and service agreements demonstrating that the physical servers are dynamically allocated, controlled by the CSP, and pooled across multiple tenants.

body.text: Cloud Computing Service Models and Nexus to Qualified Research Activities
Evaluating IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS Under the Computer Rental Provision

Because cloud service providers bundle diverse technical capabilities onto unified monthly invoices, determining whether an expenditure constitutes a payment "for the right to use computers in the conduct of qualified research" under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii) requires disaggregating cloud usage by service delivery model. Drawing on the standard technical definitions adopted by the IRS in its Cloud Computing Environment guidance and Treasury's cloud transaction preambles (REG-130700-14 and T.D. 10022), cloud offerings divide into three primary architectural tiers alongside specialized container and serverless abstractions.

Under the Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) model, the CSP provisions fundamental computing resources—processing (CPUs, GPUs, and tensor processing units), storage, networks, and virtualization—where the consumer deploys and runs arbitrary software, including operating systems and custom applications. While the consumer controls the operating systems, storage, and deployed applications (and possibly limited networking components such as host firewalls), the consumer does not manage or control the underlying physical cloud infrastructure. In practice, IaaS is the most direct modern analogue to 1980s mainframe time-sharing and readily qualifies as a computer rental QRE under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b)(4) to the extent the virtual machines or high-performance computing (HPC) clusters are directly used to conduct QRAs.

Under the Platform as a Service (PaaS) model, the CSP provides the capability to deploy consumer-created or acquired applications onto the cloud infrastructure using programming languages, libraries, services, and development tools supported by the provider. The consumer controls the deployed applications and hosting environment configuration settings, while the CSP manages the underlying network, servers, operating systems, and storage. Closely related cloud abstractions analyzed in The Tax Adviser include Containers as a Service (CaaS)—which delivers and manages hardware and software resources to develop and deploy applications using containers (packages of necessary application elements)—and Function as a Service (FaaS) or serverless computing, which allows developers to build and execute discrete snippets of code or functions on demand. Costs for PaaS, CaaS, and FaaS compute charges incurred for cloud-hosted software development platforms, staging sandboxes, automated continuous integration/continuous deployment (CI/CD) build/compile pipelines, and beta testing of pre-release software generally qualify as computer rental QREs.

By contrast, under the Software as a Service (SaaS) model, the consumer is provided access to the provider's finished software applications running on a cloud infrastructure via a thin client interface (such as a web browser) or program interface (e.g., web-based email, customer relationship management [CRM], enterprise resource planning [ERP], or collaboration suites). The consumer exercises no control over the underlying cloud infrastructure, operating systems, storage, or individual application capabilities beyond limited user-specific configuration settings. SaaS subscription costs are generally excluded from computer rental QREs because the taxpayer is paying for access to a vendor's finished commercial software service or operational platform rather than renting computing capacity to conduct its own qualified research. Furthermore, practitioner analyses note that ancillary cloud invoice line items—such as routine file storage, data migration, optical character recognition (OCR), general data security services, and financial computing management—do not constitute qualified computer rental expenses. (Some tax practitioners also point to an alternative statutory pathway under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii) where cloud expenditures used specifically to run an experimental "pilot model" are evaluated under the supply QRE rules in R&D studies, though standard cloud compute claims proceed under the computer rental rules of IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii)).
The table below synthesizes the analytical framework across specific cloud service models and operational workloads by their eligibility under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii).

body.text: Establishing Nexus to the Four-Part Test and Cost Allocation Rules

Satisfying the three structural requirements of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b)(4) is necessary but not sufficient to claim a computer rental QRE. Under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii), the computer must be used "in the conduct of qualified research". Under IRC § 41(d)(1) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(1)–(2), an activity constitutes "qualified research" only if it meets all four statutory tests, applied separately to each discrete business component under IRC § 41(d)(2)(A) (defined in IRC § 41(d)(2)(B) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(1)–(2) as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in a trade or business of the taxpayer):

items: The Section 174A / Section 174 Test (Elimination of Uncertainty): Under IRC § 41(d)(1)(A) (as amended by P.L. 119-21 § 70302 for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, and under former IRC § 41(d)(1)(A) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(2)(i) referencing IRC § 174 for prior years), expenditures with respect to the research must be eligible for treatment as domestic research or experimental expenditures under IRC § 174A (or specified research or experimental expenditures under IRC § 174 for 2022–2024). Under Treas. Reg. §§ 1.174-2(a)(1) and 1.41-4(a)(3)(i)–(ii), the research must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is intended to eliminate uncertainty concerning the capability or method for developing or improving a business component, or the appropriate design of that business component, based on information available to the taxpayer at the outset.

The Technological in Nature Test: Under IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(i) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(4), the process of experimentation used to discover the information must fundamentally rely on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science. Crucially for computer rental claims, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(7) (Use of computers and information technology) explicitly cautions that the mere employment of computers or information technology, or reliance on principles of computer science or information technology to store, collect, manipulate, translate, disseminate, produce, distribute, or process data or information, "does not itself establish that qualified research has been undertaken".

The Business Component / Permitted Purpose Test: Under IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii) and § 41(d)(3)(A), and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(ii), the application of the discovered information must be intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component of the taxpayer for a qualified purpose—specifically, a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality (expressly excluding research relating to style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors under IRC § 41(d)(3)(B)). Additionally, if software is developed primarily for internal use by the taxpayer (Internal Use Software or IUS) and does not fall within an exception under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6)(ii) (such as software developed for use in an activity that constitutes qualified research or a production process meeting IRC § 41(d)(1), or a new/improved package of software and hardware), it must also satisfy the "high threshold of innovation" (HTI) test of IRC § 41(d)(4)(E) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii) (including significant economic risk due to technical risk that resources committed to the project would not be recovered within a reasonable period).

The Process of Experimentation Test: Under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i) and (a)(6), substantially all—defined in Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6) as 80% or more of a taxpayer's research activities with respect to the business component, measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis—must constitute elements of a systematic process of experimentation designed to evaluate one or more alternatives (through modeling, simulation, or a systematic trial and error methodology) to achieve a result where the capability, method, or appropriate design is uncertain at the beginning of the research activities.

body.text: Under the last sentence of IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d)(2), if "substantially all" (at least 80%) of the services performed by an employee for the taxpayer during a taxable year consist of qualified services (engaging in, directly supervising, or directly supporting qualified research), then 100% of that employee's wages for the taxable year qualify as in-house QREs. By contrast, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b)(1) explicitly states:

"Supplies and personal property (except to the extent provided in paragraph (b)(4) of this section) are used in the conduct of qualified research if they are used in the performance of qualified services (as defined in section 41(b)(2)(B), but without regard to the last sentence thereof) by an employee of the taxpayer... Expenditures for supplies or for the use of personal property that are indirect research expenditures or general and administrative expenses do not qualify as inhouse research expenses."

By incorporating IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) "without regard to the last sentence thereof," Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b)(1) expressly bars application of the 80% wage "substantially all" safe harbor to supplies and computer rentals. (Similarly, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(7)(ii) confirms that the 80% rule of § 1.41-2(d)(2) applies only where in-house research expenses are wages). Consequently, if a cloud server cluster is utilized 85% for qualified R&D simulation and 15% for hosting live customer production workloads or corporate inventory software, the taxpayer cannot claim 100% of the server cost. The taxpayer must strictly apportion the expenditure and claim only the 85% directly attributable to qualified research.

Furthermore, two statutory exclusions under IRC § 41(d)(4) regularly govern mixed cloud environments. First, under the Commercial Production Exclusion (IRC § 41(d)(4)(A) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(2)), any activity conducted after the beginning of commercial production of a business component—defined as after the component is developed to the point where it is ready for commercial sale or use, or meets the basic functional and economic requirements of the taxpayer for the component's sale or use—is strictly excluded from qualified research, disqualifying cloud servers hosting live customer-facing production software or post-release routine maintenance. Second, under the Foreign Research Exclusion (IRC § 41(d)(4)(F) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(7)), any research conducted outside the United States (as defined in IRC § 7701(a)(9)), the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or any other possession of the United States does not constitute qualified research. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(7)(ii), in-house research expenses paid or incurred for qualified services performed both inside and outside the United States, Puerto Rico, and U.S. possessions must be strictly apportioned, and only the domestic portion is eligible. Taxpayers provisioning cloud workloads must therefore verify and document that both the R&D personnel and the physical CSP data center regions executing the R&D compute workloads are located within the United States or its territories.
Hypothetical Worked Examples: Cloud Cost Allocation and Inclusion Rate Impact
Hypothetical Example 1: Manufacturing Technology Company HPC IaaS Allocation

Assume a domestic manufacturing technology company designs a new automated production line process (a distinct business component under IRC § 41(d)(2)(B)). To resolve technical uncertainties regarding material stress and temperature tolerances at the outset of development (IRC § 41(d)(1)(A) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(3)), its U.S.-based engineers perform iterative computational fluid dynamics (CFD) and finite element analysis (FEA) simulations (a process of experimentation under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)) using on-demand high-performance computing (HPC) virtual clusters (IaaS) rented from a third-party CSP located in the United States. Neither the company nor any controlled group member receives or accrues payments from others for the right to use substantially identical personal property.

items: Total Annual Cloud IaaS Expenditure: The company incurs $500,000.00 in total IaaS charges during the taxable year.

Usage Segregation via Cloud Logs: Contemporaneous CSP usage logs and project metadata tags establish that $400,000.00 (80% of total spend: $400,000.00 ÷ $500,000.00 = 80%) was incurred directly for running iterative CFD and FEA simulations to evaluate design alternatives and eliminate technical uncertainty during the pre-production development phase, while the remaining $100,000.00 (20% of total spend: $100,000.00 ÷ $500,000.00 = 20%) was incurred for hosting the corporate marketing website and running internal inventory management software.

Qualification and Allocation Calculation: Because the CSP owns and operates the physical servers at an off-premises U.S. data center and pools hardware dynamically across multiple tenants, the three-part test of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b)(4) is satisfied. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b)(1), the 80% wage "substantially all" rule does not apply to computer rentals; thus, the $100,000.00 operational/G&A portion is strictly excluded ($0.00 QRE), and only the $400,000.00 CFD/FEA simulation portion qualifies as an in-house computer rental expense under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii).

Comparison of QRE Base and Gross Credit Impact (100% vs. 65% Inclusion): When properly classified as an in-house computer rental QRE under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii) at the 100% inclusion rate, the eligible QRE equals $400,000.00 ($400,000.00 × 100%). If instead misclassified as a general contract research expense under IRC § 41(b)(3)(A) at the 65% inclusion rate, the eligible QRE drops to $260,000.00 ($400,000.00 × 65%), sacrificing $140,000.00 (35% of the qualified expenditure) from the QRE base. Assuming the qualified expenditure represents incremental QREs above the taxpayer's base amount prior to any IRC § 280C(c) adjustment, proper classification as computer rental yields $80,000.00 in gross credit ($400,000.00 × 20%) versus $52,000.00 ($260,000.00 × 20%) under the 20% Regular Credit method of IRC § 41(a)(1) (preserving $28,000.00 in gross tax credit), and yields $56,000.00 in gross credit ($400,000.00 × 14%) versus $36,400.00 ($260,000.00 × 14%) under the 14% Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) method of IRC § 41(c)(4)(A) (preserving $19,600.00 in gross tax credit).

body.text: Hypothetical Example 2: Software Company "Cloud Split" Cost Segregation

Assume a domestic software company incurs $100,000.00 in annual cloud computing charges across four distinct operational environments. First, its Dev/Test Environment (EC2 instances used exclusively for pre-release beta testing) and Compile Servers (automated software build pipelines) account for 65% of total cloud usage, or $65,000.00 ($100,000.00 × 65%). Because these environments are physically located off-premises in U.S. data centers, owned and operated by the CSP in a multi-tenant resource pool, and directly used by software engineers in systematic code experimentation and build verification prior to commercial release, the entire $65,000.00 qualifies at a 100% inclusion rate as an in-house Computer Rental QRE under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii). Second, its Production Hosting (hosting the live commercial SaaS application for paying customers) and Corporate Admin (Office 365 / G-Suite corporate email and standard file storage) account for the remaining 35% of total cloud usage, or $35,000.00 ($100,000.00 × 35%). Live customer production hosting is excluded as post-commercial production activity under IRC § 41(d)(4)(A) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(2), while corporate email and routine file storage are excluded as G&A expenses and end-user SaaS consumption under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b)(1), resulting in $0.00 in eligible QREs from this $35,000.00 segment.
Documentation, Form 6765 Compliance, and Audit Defense
Revised Form 6765 and Section G Business Component Reporting
The IRS has substantially redesigned Form 6765 (Credit for Increasing Research Activities) to require front-end transparency and business-component-level disaggregation of QREs.

On the revised Form 6765, individual expense lines—including computer rental costs—have been moved out of Sections A and B into the new Section F (Qualified Research Expenses Summary) and Section G (Business Component Information). Section F begins with Item A, which asks: "Are you required to complete Section G? See instructions to determine if you are required to complete Section G, and how to complete Section F if you are not required to complete Section G". Taxpayers that complete Section G must report the qualified rental or lease cost of computers separately for each reported business component in Section G, Line/Column 55 ("Rental or lease cost of computers"). The sum of Column 55 across all reported business components (including any attachments and the aggregate business components row) is then carried to Section F, Line 44 ("Total rental or lease cost of computers for all business components"). Taxpayers that are not required to complete Section G (and do not opt to complete it voluntarily) enter their total qualified computer rental or lease costs directly on Section F, Line 44. On Section F, Line 48, the total rental or lease cost of computers on Line 44 is summed with total qualified wages (Line 42), total costs of supplies (Line 43), and total applicable contract research and basic research payments (Line 47, which adds Lines 45 and 46), and the resulting total QREs on Line 48 are carried to Line 5 (Regular Credit) or Line 20 (Alternative Simplified Credit). For members of a controlled group filing separate tax returns, the IRS Instructions for Form 6765 explicitly require each member to report on Line 44 and Column 55 only that individual member's qualified rental or lease cost of computers, not the combined controlled-group total.

First, regarding the mandatory effective date, the verbatim IRS Instructions for Form 6765 state: "For tax years beginning before 2026, Section G will be optional for all filers... For tax years beginning after 2025, Section G will be required, subject to the guidelines in Section G—Business Component Information". Thus, Section G remains optional on timely filed original returns for the 2024 and 2025 tax years and becomes mandatory only starting with the 2026 tax year.

Second, even for tax years beginning after 2025, the IRS Instructions for Form 6765 exempt a taxpayer from completing Section G if it satisfies specific statutory or administrative criteria. Under the Qualified Small Business (QSB) Payroll Tax Credit Exemption, a taxpayer is exempt from Section G if it is a QSB as defined under IRC § 41(h)(3) and checks the box on Form 6765 to claim the reduced payroll tax credit under IRC § 41(h)(1)–(2). Under the Small QREs and Gross Receipts Exemption, a taxpayer claiming the research credit on an original return is exempt from Section G if its total QREs determined at the controlled-group level are equal to or less than $1.5 million and its average annual gross receipts for the prior three tax years (determined under IRC § 448(c)(3) without regard to subparagraph (A)) are equal to or less than $50 million. (While a cited Thomson Reuters blog post erroneously stated "$15 million in gross receipts," the authoritative IRS Instructions for Form 6765 and EY Tax News analysis confirm the gross receipts threshold is $50 million.) Additionally, taxpayers eligible to follow the Large Business and International (LB&I) ASC 730 Directive (checking "Yes" on Line 41) make a single entry of "ASC 730 Directive" in Section G, Column 49(c) and are exempt from itemizing additional individual business components in Section G if their ASC 730 Directive QREs equal at least 80% of total Line 48 QREs.

Third, for taxpayers required to complete Section G, the IRS instructions establish the "80% / Top 50" business components rule, under which filers must itemize business components in descending order of total QREs until the reported components account for at least 80% of total QREs, capped at a maximum of 50 business components (even if those 50 components constitute less than 80% of total QREs, and even if the taxpayer uses statistical sampling under Rev. Proc. 2011-42). All remaining business components outside the 80% / Top 50 threshold are combined on a single line by entering "Aggregate Business Components" (or "Aggregate BCs") in Column 49(c), reporting their combined QREs across Columns 50 through 56 (including aggregate computer rental costs in Column 55), and leaving Columns 49(a), 49(b), 49(d), 49(e), and 49(f) blank. Furthermore, while Column 49(f) is titled "Describe the information sought to be discovered", the official Form 6765 instructions specify that completing Column 49(f) is required only if the taxpayer is claiming a refund or credit on an amended return with an IRC § 41 credit that was not reported on the original return or is increased from the original return. Filers are not required to complete Column 49(f) on timely filed original returns (including extensions), though narrative substantiation remains subject to request upon IRS examination.

body.text: Substantiation Methodologies, Cloud Tagging, and Judicial Precedent

Under IRC § 6001 and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d) (promulgated in T.D. 9104, 69 FR 22, Jan. 2, 2004, applicable to taxable years ending on or after December 31, 2003), a taxpayer claiming a credit under IRC § 41 must retain records in sufficiently usable form and detail to substantiate that the expenditures claimed are eligible for the credit. In the context of computer rental QREs, IRS examiners and tax practitioners emphasize that general ledger account balances, CSP master service agreements, and summary monthly cloud invoices only confirm that an expense was paid or incurred—they do not establish how the computing capacity was used, which employees accessed it, or which business component it supported.

Because public cloud billing is consumption-based and commingles eligible R&D compute charges with ineligible storage, security, and live production hosting on a single invoice, retrospective manual estimation is highly vulnerable during an IRS examination. To construct an audit-ready substantiation trail, taxpayers should implement three operational controls:

items: Cloud-Native Metadata Tagging: Configure mandatory resource tagging within the CSP console (such as AWS cost allocation tags, Azure resource groups, or Google Cloud labels) prior to provisioning instances so that every virtual machine, container cluster, or build server carries immutable metadata tags identifying: (a) the Environment Type (Development, QA, Staging, or Simulation vs. Production or Corporate Admin), (b) the Business Component / R&D Project ID (mapping directly to Form 6765, Section G, Column 49(c)), and (c) the CSP Data Center Region (verifying domestic U.S. location under IRC § 41(d)(4)(F) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(7)).

Automated Telemetry and API Usage Logs: Export contemporaneous CSP billing and telemetry logs via API integrations to generate granular schedules documenting exact compute hours, CPU/GPU utilization, dynamic multi-tenant server allocation, and dollar charges by project tag. As highlighted in analysis from Thomson Reuters, corporate tax departments increasingly pair these telemetry logs with enterprise generative AI (GenAI) documentation tools to ingest engineering sprint tickets, code commit histories, and test logs, translating contemporaneous technical records into Section G business component summaries.

Technical Nexus Mapping and Contract Verification: Link employee R&D time tracking and sprint documentation directly to the tagged cloud environments (establishing that the rented computers were used by employees in the performance of qualified services under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b)(1)), document the terms of the cloud contract to show that the CSP operates and dynamically controls the physical servers under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b)(4), and verify third-party customer contracts to confirm the taxpayer retains substantial rights to the research results and is not performing excluded "funded research" under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d).

body.text: In Phoenix Design Group, the IRS disallowed IRC § 41 research credits claimed by a mechanical, electrical, plumbing, and fire protection (MEPF) engineering firm that were generated during the tax years ended December 31, 2013, through December 31, 2016 ($138,205 in 2013; $158,031 in 2014; $138,334 in 2015; and $128,228 in 2016) and carried forward and utilized on returns for the 2015 through 2019 tax years ($55,504 utilized in 2015; $47,811 in 2016; $219,177 in 2017; $68,147 in 2018; and $71,102 in 2019). Out of a total pool of 238 projects, the parties tried a judgment sample of three specific building projects: (1) the Gerald Champion Military Psychiatric Unit (Project No. 13008.00), (2) the Baptist Memorial Hospital–North Mississippi (Oxford) / Baptist Memorial Health North Mississippi Oxford project (BMHNMO / BHNM Oxford, Project No. 13003.00), and (3) the Vanderbilt University Engineering and Science Building (VUESB, Project No. 12010.01).

The Tax Court disallowed 100% of the claimed research credits across all three sampled projects and sustained a 20% accuracy-related penalty under IRC § 6662 across the 2015–2019 utilization years ($11,101 for 2015; $9,021 for 2016; $43,835 for 2017; $13,629 for 2018; and $14,220 for 2019) per the parties' stipulation. First, on the Section 174 / 174A elimination-of-uncertainty test, the court rejected the taxpayer's contention that design uncertainty existed merely because the footprint of a building or final equipment selections (such as for a hybrid operating room) might change until construction was completed; relying on standard engineering calculations, historical data, or compliance with building codes where schematic block diagrams already established the basic system design did not demonstrate objective technical uncertainty at the outset under IRC § 41(d)(1)(A) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(3). Second, on the process of experimentation test, connecting work to a linear six-stage American Institute of Architects (AIA) design process or applying professional expertise to preliminary computations did not constitute an evaluative, hypothesis-driven process of experimentation evaluating alternatives under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5). Third, employee timesheets contained generic phase narratives (such as "design" or "coordination") that failed to tie specific hours or calculations to defined technical uncertainties or distinguish between the roles of mechanical, electrical, or plumbing engineers and CAD designers. Fourth, under the "shrinking-back" rule of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2), if an overall business component fails the four-part test of IRC § 41(d)(1), the requirements are applied to the most significant subset of elements of the product or process until a qualifying subcomponent is reached. In Phoenix Design Group, the Tax Court held that because the taxpayer failed to maintain contemporaneous, subcomponent-level documentation demonstrating how uncertainty in a discrete element created uncertainty or was systematically resolved, the court could not apply the shrinking-back rule to salvage any portion of the credit. For taxpayers claiming cloud computer rental QREs, Phoenix Design Group demonstrates that claiming a flat percentage of an AWS or Azure invoice based on high-level management estimates—without contemporaneous usage logs and test records showing that specific compute instances executed an iterative evaluation of technical alternatives for a documented business component or subcomponent—carries severe disallowance and IRC § 6662 penalty exposure.
Base Period Consistency Requirement (IRC Section 41(c)(5) and Formerly Section 41(c)(6))

Because the IRC § 41 research credit is an incremental tax incentive that rewards increases in QREs over a historical baseline, taxpayers adding cloud computing or computer rental expenses to their current-year QREs must comply with the statutory base period consistency rule. Auditing the statutory history and regulatory text clarifies both the exact Code citation and the mathematical direction of the base period adjustment.

First, regarding statutory codification, the consistency requirement is currently codified at IRC § 41(c)(5) (Consistent treatment of expenses required). (Prior to the enactment of the old Alternative Incremental Credit, the consistency rule was originally codified at IRC § 41(c)(5), as reflected in Treas. Reg. § 1.41-3(d)(2) Example 1 promulgated in 2001; it was subsequently redesignated as IRC § 41(c)(6), as reflected in Treas. Reg. § 1.41-9(c)(2) promulgated in 2011; and when Congress repealed the expired Alternative Incremental Credit in 2014, it was redesignated back to IRC § 41(c)(5) in the current United States Code). Under IRC § 41(c)(5)(A), notwithstanding whether the period for filing a claim for credit or refund has expired for any taxable year taken into account in determining the fixed-base percentage, the QREs taken into account in computing such percentage must be determined on a basis consistent with the determination of QREs for the credit year.

The consistency requirement operates across both statutory calculation methods. Under the Regular Credit Method (IRC § 41(a)(1), § 41(c)(1)–(3), and § 41(c)(5); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-3(d)(1)–(2)), the credit equals 20% of the excess of current-year QREs over the "base amount" (the product of the taxpayer's fixed-base percentage and its average annual gross receipts for the four preceding taxable years, subject to a minimum base amount of 50% of current-year QREs under IRC § 41(c)(2) and a maximum fixed-base percentage of 16% under IRC § 41(c)(3)(C)). For legacy taxpayers, the fixed-base percentage is the ratio of aggregate QREs to aggregate gross receipts for taxable years beginning after December 31, 1983, and before January 1, 1989 (the 1984–1988 fixed-base period), whereas startup companies follow the phased-in rules of IRC § 41(c)(3)(B). Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-3(d)(1) (promulgated in T.D. 8930, Jan. 3, 2001), QREs and gross receipts taken into account in computing the fixed-base percentage and base amount must be determined on a basis consistent with the definition of QREs and gross receipts for the credit year, without regard to the law in effect during the base years and even if the statute of limitations for those base years has expired. As explicitly illustrated in Treas. Reg. § 1.41-3(d)(2), Example 2, if a taxpayer claims in the credit year that a certain type of expenditure is a QRE—reflecting a change in position because the taxpayer had not previously claimed similar expenditures as QREs—the consistency rule requires the taxpayer to adjust its base period QREs to include any similar expenditures incurred during the fixed-base period. Similarly, under the Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) Method (IRC § 41(c)(4); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-9(c)(2)), the credit equals 14% of the amount by which current-year QREs exceed 50% of the average QREs for the three taxable years preceding the credit year (or 6% of current-year QREs under IRC § 41(c)(4)(B) if the taxpayer had no QREs in any of the three preceding taxable years). Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-9(c)(2) (promulgated in T.D. 9528, 76 FR 33996, June 10, 2011), QREs for the three taxable years preceding the credit year must likewise be determined on a basis consistent with the definition of QREs for the credit year, without regard to the law in effect for those three preceding years and even if the period for filing a claim for credit or refund has expired for any of those three prior years.

When a taxpayer begins claiming cloud computing or computer rental expenses as QREs in the credit year, including analogous computer rental expenses incurred during the historical base years adjusts the base period QREs and the resulting base amount upward (not downward). Mathematically, because the incremental credit is computed by subtracting the base amount from current-year QREs—either as 20% × (Current-Year QREs − Base Amount) under the Regular Credit or 14% × (Current-Year QREs − [50% × Average QREs of Prior 3 Years]) under the ASC—increasing the historical base period QREs increases the subtracted base amount, which in turn adjusts the current-year net incremental credit downward to prevent an artificially inflated growth rate.
Policy, Regulatory, and Legislative Developments Requiring Clarification
Modernizing Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(b)(4) and the Impact of T.D. 10022 (Treasury Regulation Section 1.861-19)

While the IRS and tax practitioners generally accept multi-tenant public cloud IaaS and PaaS development and testing environments under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b)(4), several structural ambiguities persist when applying the 1989 three-part test to contemporary R&D environments.

First, the term "computer" is never formally defined in IRC § 41 or its underlying regulations. In the context of MACRS depreciation, IRC § 168(i)(2)(B)(ii) (see also Asset Class 00.12, Information Systems, of Rev. Proc. 87-56) defines a "computer" as a programmable electronically activated device that (I) is capable of accepting information, applying prescribed processes to the information, and supplying the results of the processes with or without human intervention, and (II) consists of a central processing unit containing extensive storage, logic, arithmetic, and control capabilities. Meanwhile, "computer software" is defined separately in IRC § 197(e)(3)(B) (added in 1993) as "any program designed to cause a computer to perform a desired function". In modern R&D, software and cloud abstractions (IaaS, CaaS, PaaS, FaaS, and SaaS) perform the functional role once occupied by physical 1980s mainframes, and accessing a computer under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii) ("the right to use computers") naturally encompasses the use of software. Second, consider a taxpayer that cannot afford to develop specialized research software and therefore leases the software from an unrelated vendor (acquiring no ownership rights and no access to the source code), but due to cybersecurity or regulatory mandates hosts the leased software locally on its own internal servers. From a legislative-intent perspective under the Tax Reform Act of 1986, renting specialized computing capability for research should qualify; yet under the literal text of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b)(4), hosting the leased software on internal servers risks failing both the "owned and operated by someone other than the taxpayer" prong and the "located off the taxpayer's premises" prong. Third, because CSPs restrict customer visibility into physical server utilization across other tenants for security reasons ("location independence" under the IRS Cloud Computing Environment definition of resource pooling), taxpayers cannot independently measure whether their workload exceeded 50% of a specific physical server blade's time without administrative safe harbors confirming that standard on-demand or multi-tenant cloud contracts satisfy the non-primary user requirement.

Auditing the primary Federal Register and Internal Revenue Bulletin releases reveals a critical legal tension that taxpayers and policymakers must navigate. On January 14, 2025, the Treasury Department and the IRS published T.D. 10022 (Classification of Digital Content Transactions and Cloud Transactions, 90 FR 2977; 2025-8 I.R.B. 773), finalizing Treas. Reg. §§ 1.861-18 and 1.861-19, effective January 14, 2025. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.861-19(b), a "cloud transaction" is defined as a transaction through which a person obtains on-demand network access to computer hardware, digital content (as defined in § 1.861-18(a)(2)), or other similar resources—encompassing IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS. Crucially, abandoning the multifactor lease-versus-service analysis (including IRC § 7701(e) factors) that had been proposed in the August 2019 proposed regulations (REG-130700-14, 84 FR 40317), final Treas. Reg. § 1.861-19(c)(1) classifies all cloud transactions solely as the provision of services and never as a lease of property, reasoning that the cloud provider retains economic control and possession over the physical servers and software and has authority to replace the property used to provide the transaction. Furthermore, for multi-element transactions (such as a cloud transaction combined with a digital content download), Treas. Reg. §§ 1.861-18(b)(3) and 1.861-19(c)(2) replace the former de minimis rule with a "predominant character" rule determined by the primary benefit or value to the customer (or to a typical customer based on actual usage data under § 1.861-18(b)(3)(ii)).

However, Section VI of the preamble to T.D. 10022 ("Final Regulations Apply Only for Certain International Provisions of the Code") explicitly restricts the applicability of Treas. Reg. §§ 1.861-18 and 1.861-19 to enumerated international tax provisions of the Internal Revenue Code—specifically Subchapter N of Chapter 1, and IRC §§ 59A, 245A, 250, 267A, 367, 404A, 482, 679, 842, 845, 1059A, and Chapters 3 and 4. Thus, T.D. 10022 does not currently govern IRC § 41. Concurrently with T.D. 10022, Treasury and the IRS issued Notice 2025-6 (Request for Comments on Applying the Characterization Rules in §§ 1.861-18 and 1.861-19 to All Provisions of the Internal Revenue Code, 2025-8 I.R.B. 799), formally soliciting public comments on the consequences, interactions, and needed guidance if the characterization rules of Treas. Reg. §§ 1.861-18 and 1.861-19 were extended to apply to all provisions of the Code (listing specific sections such as IRC §§ 167(f), 168(g)(1)(B), 178, 197, 263, 263A, 451, 471, 856–859, 1001, 1011, 1221, 1222, and 1241, as well as general Code-wide interactions).

From an R&D tax audit perspective, if Treasury were to extend Treas. Reg. § 1.861-19's blanket characterization of cloud transactions as the "provision of services" (rather than a lease of property) across the entire Code pursuant to Notice 2025-6 without concurrently updating Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b)(4) or carving out IRC § 41, IRS examiners could contend that IaaS and PaaS payments are service payments (either disqualified as non-research hosting services or capped at 65% as contract research under IRC § 41(b)(3)(A)) rather than payments for "the right to use computers" (reported on Form 6765 as "rental or lease cost of computers") under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii). Because the statutory text of IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii) uses the flexible phrase "any amount paid or incurred to another person for the right to use computers in the conduct of qualified research"—making no mention of common-law lease characterization under IRC § 7701(e), hardware ownership, or physical mainframe location—Treasury possesses express statutory authority under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii) to modernize Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b)(4) using a substance-over-form approach that explicitly confirms on-demand cloud computing (IaaS, PaaS, CaaS, and FaaS) used directly in qualified research as a 100% in-house QRE.
Standardizing Defensible Cloud Allocation Methodologies

In multi-tenant and containerized cloud environments, data and compute workloads frequently commingle across shared virtual clusters—a technical challenge the IRS itself recognizes in its Cloud Computing Environment guidance when addressing commingled Federal Tax Information (FTI) under IRS Publication 1075 (which mandates strict data-element labeling and system/application-level audit trails). Under the final sentence of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d), Treasury and the IRS have express regulatory authority to agree with taxpayers on specific recordkeeping guidelines for substantiating research credits. Issuing an administrative revenue procedure or updated Audit Techniques Guide chapter that formally recognizes cloud-native metadata tagging (by environment type and Section G business component ID), automated CI/CD build/compile telemetry logs, and proportional developer-hour allocation ratios as compliant substantiation methods under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b)(1) would substantially reduce audit friction for both taxpayers and IRS examiners.
Interplay Between IRC Section 41 Computer Rental QREs and IRC Sections 174 and 174A

However, on July 4, 2025, Congress enacted Public Law 119-21 (139 Stat. 72, § 70302, 139 Stat. 189, commonly known as the One, Big, Beautiful Bill Act or OBBBA), which fundamentally overhauled the tax treatment of domestic R&E expenditures and repealed mandatory five-year domestic amortization for post-2024 taxable years.

items: Immediate Expensing or Elective Amortization of Domestic R&E Under IRC § 174A (Post-2024 Tax Years): Section 70302(a) of Public Law 119-21 added IRC § 174A (Domestic Research or Experimental Expenditures), effective for amounts paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024. Under IRC § 174A(a), taxpayers are permitted to immediately deduct 100% of "domestic research or experimental expenditures" (defined in IRC § 174A(b) as R&E expenditures paid or incurred in connection with the taxpayer's trade or business, excluding expenditures attributable to foreign research under IRC § 41(d)(4)(F)) during the taxable year in which paid or incurred, notwithstanding IRC § 263. Adopting IRC § 174A(a) for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, is treated as an automatic change in method of accounting under IRC § 481 applied on a cut-off basis with no IRC § 481(a) adjustment. Alternatively, under IRC § 174A(c) and Section 6.02 of Rev. Proc. 2025-28, a taxpayer may elect to charge domestic R&E expenditures (not chargeable to depreciable or depletable property) to a capital account and amortize them ratably over a period of not less than 60 months, beginning with the month in which the taxpayer first realizes benefits from such expenditures. To make this election, the taxpayer attaches a statement titled "FILED PURSUANT TO SECTION 6.02 OF REV. PROC. 2025-28" to its original federal income tax return by the due date (including extensions), and the election is binding for the election year and all subsequent years unless consent to change is obtained. Under IRC § 174A(d)(3), any amount paid or incurred in connection with the development of any software continues to be treated as a research or experimental expenditure. Under IRC § 174A(d)(1), while capital expenditures for the acquisition or improvement of land or depreciable property are excluded from IRC § 174A, annual allowances for depreciation under IRC § 167 on property used in connection with domestic R&E are treated as domestic R&E expenditures under IRC § 174A (even though depreciation remains excluded from IRC § 41 supply and computer rental QREs under IRC § 41(b)(2)(C)(ii) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b)(4)).

Continued 15-Year Mandatory Amortization for Foreign R&E Under Amended IRC § 174: Section 70302(b)(1) of Public Law 119-21 amended IRC § 174 so that, for amounts paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, IRC § 174 applies exclusively to foreign research or experimental expenditures (expenditures attributable to research conducted outside the United States, Puerto Rico, or U.S. territories within the meaning of IRC § 41(d)(4)(F)). Foreign R&E expenditures—such as cloud computing workloads executed on foreign servers or by foreign R&D personnel—remain completely ineligible for the IRC § 41 research credit under IRC § 41(d)(4)(F) and must be capitalized and amortized ratably over a 15-year period beginning with the midpoint of the taxable year under amended IRC § 174. Furthermore, under IRC § 174(d) as amended by OBBBA § 70302(b)(1)(C) (effective for property disposed of, retired, or abandoned after May 12, 2025), if property associated with foreign R&E expenditures is disposed of, retired, or abandoned during the 15-year amortization period, no deduction or reduction to the amount realized is permitted on account of such event, and the 15-year amortization schedule must continue.

Transitional Relief for 2022–2024 Capitalized Domestic SRE Expenditures (OBBBA § 70302(f) & Rev. Proc. 2025-28): For domestic SRE expenditures (including cloud computer rental and software development costs) that were previously capitalized and amortized under TCJA § 174 during taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, and before January 1, 2025, OBBBA § 70302(f) and Rev. Proc. 2025-28 provide two major transition pathways. First, under OBBBA § 70302(f)(2) and Section 7.02 of Rev. Proc. 2025-23 (as modified by Rev. Proc. 2025-28 and Rev. Proc. 2026-32), any taxpayer holding remaining unamortized domestic SRE balances previously capitalized under TCJA § 174 may make an automatic accounting method change to deduct those remaining unamortized balances either entirely in its first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024 (the 2025 tax year) or ratably over a two-year period (the 2025 and 2026 tax years). Second, under OBBBA § 70302(f)(1), an eligible small business taxpayer—defined as a taxpayer (other than a tax shelter under IRC § 448(d)(3)) that meets the IRC § 448(c) gross receipts test for its first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024 (requiring prior three-year average annual gross receipts of $31,000,000 or less as adjusted for inflation for 2025 by Rev. Proc. 2024-40)—may elect to apply IRC § 174A and amended IRC § 280C(c)(1) retroactively to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, and before January 1, 2025. Under Rev. Proc. 2025-28, an eligible small business may implement this retroactive election either by filing amended returns or Administrative Adjustment Requests (AARs) for the 2022–2024 tax years on or before the earlier of July 6, 2026 (since July 4, 2026, is a Saturday under IRC § 7503) or the expiration of the IRC § 6511 statute of limitations, or by filing an automatic accounting method change statement (Designated Change Number 273) in lieu of Form 3115 with a modified IRC § 481(a) adjustment. Rev. Proc. 2025-28 also granted an automatic six-month extension under IRC § 6081 for eligible taxpayers that had already filed 2024 returns prior to September 15, 2025, to file superseding 2024 returns labeled "REVENUE PROCEDURE 2025-28".

Distinguishing Section 174 / 174A Software and Cloud Costs from Section 41 QREs (Notice 2023-63) and Section 280C(c) Coordination: For determining which software development and property rent/lease costs fall within the broader scope of IRC §§ 174 and 174A, the IRS previously issued interim guidance in Notice 2023-63 (2023-39 I.R.B. 919, modified by Notice 2024-12, 2024-5 I.R.B. 616). Section 5.02(1) of Notice 2023-63 defines "computer software" broadly to include system, programming, application, and embedded software, whether stored locally or accessed remotely via cloud computing, and Section 5.01 renders Section 5 of Rev. Proc. 2000-50 obsolete. Crucially, Section 1 of Notice 2023-63 explicitly states that while its rules affect whether expenditures are treated as R&E expenditures for the gateway test of IRC § 41(d)(1)(A) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(2)(i), Notice 2023-63 "is not intended to change the rules for determining eligibility for or computation of the research credit under § 41 and the regulations thereunder, including rules for 'research with respect to computer software,' and the definitions of 'qualified research' and 'qualified research expenses'". Thus, broader cloud hosting, overhead, or equipment rent/depreciation expenses that may be deductible under IRC § 174A (or capitalized under TCJA § 174) do not automatically qualify as computer rental QREs under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii) unless they independently satisfy Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b)(1) and (b)(4). Finally, because OBBBA restored immediate domestic expensing under IRC § 174A(a), OBBBA § 70302(b)(2)(B) amended IRC § 280C(c)(1) for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, to require that any domestic R&E deduction under IRC § 174A(a) (or capitalized amount under § 174A(c)) be reduced by the full amount of the IRC § 41(a) research credit allowed, unless the taxpayer makes a timely, irrevocable election under IRC § 280C(c)(2) on its original return to claim a reduced research credit.
